bodyHtml:
1.2 Instruments Overview

Why This Matters

Many beginners say, “I want to trade gold,” or “I want to trade the stock market,” before they know what product they are actually using.

That is a problem because the same market idea can be reached through very different products, with very different rules.

This lesson teaches one core idea:

first understand the market, then understand the product used to reach it

What You Should Understand After This Lesson

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:

  • name the main market families a beginner is likely to see;
  • explain the difference between an underlying market and a wrapper;
  • spot where extra caution is needed before using a product.

The Main Market Families

Market family What it gives you exposure to Common access routes Main beginner caution
Foreign exchange (FX) One currency compared with another spot FX, FX futures, CFDs leverage and spread costs
Stocks / equities Shares in individual companies shares, ETFs, options, CFDs company-specific risk
Indices A basket of many stocks cash index references, ETFs, futures, CFDs confusing the index with the wrapper
Metals Gold, silver, copper and other metals spot references, ETFs, futures, options, CFDs same metal name, different product rules
Energy Oil, gas, power-related markets futures, options, CFDs, ETFs in some regions benchmark differences like WTI vs Brent
Agriculture Corn, wheat, coffee, cocoa and more mainly futures and options seasonality and contract structure
Bonds / rates Government debt and interest-rate exposure cash bonds, bond ETFs, bond futures, options price and yield are not the same thing
Options A right to buy or sell something at a set price listed options, OTC options premium can be lost in full
Crypto Digital assets and token-based markets spot, futures, perpetuals, ETFs in some regions, DeFi custody, leverage, and venue risk

(Table alt-text: A beginner market map showing major asset classes, what each one gives exposure to, common product wrappers, and the main warning a beginner should focus on first.)

The Difference Between a Market and a Wrapper

This is the most important idea in the lesson.

  • The market is the thing you want exposure to.
  • The wrapper is the product you actually trade.

Three Short Terms You Should Know Here

  • ETF = exchange-traded fund
  • CFD = contract for difference, a broker-offered wrapper in many regions
  • OTC = over the counter, meaning trading happens through dealers or broker networks rather than one single central exchange

Example 1: The S&P 500

  • The market idea is the S&P 500 index.
  • The wrapper might be:
    • an ETF,
    • a futures contract,
    • a CFD,
    • an option on an ETF or future.

All of those point toward the same theme, but they do not behave the same way in fees, leverage, hours, expiry, or settlement.

Example 2: Gold

  • The market idea is gold.
  • The wrapper might be:
    • a gold ETF,
    • a futures contract,
    • a spot-style product,
    • a broker CFD.

So saying “I trade gold” is not enough information. A careful trader asks:

  • Which gold product?
  • Which venue?
  • Which rules?

A Simple Global View

This course is not built around one country alone.

A beginner should know that global markets include:

  • FX trading across Asia, Europe, the Middle East, and the Americas;
  • stock indices such as the S&P 500, DAX, FTSE 100, Nikkei 225, and Hang Seng;
  • metals and energy benchmarks such as gold, WTI crude, and Brent crude;
  • government bond and rate products that respond to central-bank policy in different regions.

The exact product available to a learner may depend on where they live and what type of account or broker they use. That is why understanding structure comes before choosing a product.

A Safer Learning Order for Beginners

A beginner does not need to learn every market at once.

A simpler order is:

  1. major FX pairs and major stock indices;
  2. metals and energy benchmarks;
  3. simple futures concepts;
  4. basic options language;
  5. crypto only after the main market map is clear.

This order matches the parent-folder rule that early modules should stay easy to digest.

Worked Example: "I Want to Trade Oil"

A beginner says, “I want to trade oil.”

That still leaves several unanswered questions:

  • Do they mean WTI or Brent?
  • Are they using a futures contract, ETF, or CFD?
  • Does the product expire?
  • Does the product include overnight financing?

The same market idea can lead to very different costs and risks.

That is why a good first habit is not “Which chart looks exciting?”

It is:

What is the underlying market, and what product am I actually trading?

Crypto Needs Extra Caution

Crypto belongs in the market map, but it should not be treated as a beginner shortcut.

A beginner needs to understand that crypto products can involve:

  • large price swings;
  • liquidation risk in leveraged products;
  • exchange and custody risk;
  • smart-contract risk in DeFi;
  • different legal treatment across countries.

So crypto should be understood as a separate, higher-caution part of the map, not as a replacement for learning basic market structure.

Common Beginner Mistakes

Mistake 1: Confusing the Index With the ETF

An index is the benchmark idea. An ETF is one tradable product that may track that idea.

Mistake 2: Thinking the Same Asset Name Means the Same Rules

“Gold,” “oil,” or “Bitcoin” can appear in very different products with very different mechanics.

Mistake 3: Choosing the Most Leveraged Product First

Beginners often pick the product that looks fastest or cheapest before understanding the risk.

Mistake 4: Thinking All Products Are Global in the Same Way

Some products are centralized on exchanges. Some are OTC. Some depend heavily on the broker or platform offering them.

quizItems.prompt: Which choice is best described as a wrapper that provides exposure to an underlying market rather than being the underlying market itself?
quizItems.explanation: An ETF is a tradable wrapper. It can track an underlying basket or index, but it is not the same thing as the underlying market itself.

quizItems.prompt: Which market is most commonly described as primarily OTC rather than centralized on one exchange?
quizItems.explanation: Spot FX is generally described as an OTC market, while the others are primarily exchange-traded examples.

quizItems.prompt: Why should a beginner learn the underlying market before choosing a product wrapper?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Because wrappers always reduce risk to zero

choices.label: B
choices.text: Because the same underlying can behave differently across fees, leverage, expiry, and settlement rules

choices.label: C
choices.text: Because wrappers are illegal in most regions

choices.label: D
choices.text: Because only professionals can trade ETFs

correctAnswer.label: B
correctAnswer.text: Because the same underlying can behave differently across fees, leverage, expiry, and settlement rules

quizItems.explanation: The underlying theme may be similar, but the trading mechanics can differ a lot across wrappers.
